review_text: Unfortunately the experience with Full Tour was not good and I will leave here recorded the reasons in trying to help other travellers make their own personal considerations when choosing an agency for such an important time when their holidays, rests, etc. Unfortunately, maybe in part even due to lack of a sharper assessment on my part, I did not notice that Full Tour, as well as other agencies in Santiago, are working on a scheme to close the tours and subcontract other third companies to perform the same. In my case, the tour to Isla Negra was made in a group of 8 people (4 couples, all Brazilians) where only I had closed the tour with the Full Tour (other 2 couples closed with another agency and the other couple with a different third agency) that is, there were 3 different agencies on that tour. The Guide Fernanda is the only positive point of this bad experience: Although she did not pass so much historical information about the places, she made every effort to be kind and make our experience a little better, in addition to remediing the embarrassing situation we went through (I will detail below). She is a love and had no responsibility for what happened. When we closed the tour with the Full Tour, I chose them because the tour included entries to the museum of Pablo Neruda's house in Isla Negra, which was the main goal of our tour (my wife loves the work of Pablo Neruda and we wanted to know the museum and the house in detail). When we arrived at Isla Negra, we were surprised by the information that the other 6 people in the VAN did not have these entries and that they would take a walk by the beach and local craft trade, with nothing to do with our tour. Fernanda asked me to "try to make the ride in 40 minutes at most so as not to delay lunch or the other people at the VAN". How can you sell different tours within the same tour???? Conclusion: The visit to the museum is guided and by audio and as the house is small, only 15 people enter at a time. The visit took about 1 hour and 20 minutes because we did everything running and without taking advantage of all the information from the local audio Guide, leaving us stressed and frustrated and still ashamed to have bothered the other 6 people who stood at the museum door waiting for us (think of passing all were some loves and understood what happened because I explained everything to them and they were surprised how they can organize different tours within the same tour). So here is my record and advise the other travellers not to take a tour with companies that outsource their tours. They preferred companies that do tours with their own cars and guides (including the van of this outsourced ride was horrible, old, with air running badly and the driver running like a crazy to the point of a couple asking him to maneuver in speed because they were afraid). I really didn't pay attention to it (in doubt, ask before closing) and I would never imagine that companies freeze a van with people doing different tours (or everyone should go to the museum or nobody should go and not they stay waiting for me or I have to run to keep nobody waiting). Confusing situation provided by the Full Tour. Wine tasting is outside with limited seating at Indomita.

review_text: I walked from town out to this archaeological site, a healthy 3 to 5 kilometers or so. One must watch for the signs and keep going. At one point I thought I had reached the site, only to learn I was at a campgrounds where locals were gathering to continue their several-day celebration of the Virgin Candelaria. It was a happy accident, as I got to see some of the dancers in their vibrant costumes and to hear some of the bands playing. When you reach the site, the staff is very kind, making sure you've had water in the heat. Then you begin your climb -- up the steps and along the hill paths built into the mountainside. Signs offer insights into the horrors that occurred when the locals stood up to the Spaniards, attempting to resist having to change their ways. The preservation of the buildings that have been uncovered is impressive. At the back end of the archaeological site is a small cantina where there is more historic information and examples of clothing and items used by the early people who lived centuries ago. It offers water and some other items along with a welcome respite from the heat. Continuing out the back/side door, you find the trail that begins to wind its way via competing hairpin turns up and up and up a neighboring "hill" that first takes you to a monument offering a poem by Chile's first poet laureate Gabriela Mistral, and then continues through a portal to guide you further upward to another monument where the views are spectacular. The same volcanoes viewed at the Geysers del Tatio earlier in the day appear in a wholly different perspective from this hillside. The walk (or bike ride or car/taxi trip) is worth doing. And the site is not on most people's radar, so you really get to take in the site/sights at a pace that's comfortable to you.

The operator offered to do the tour for $100 more if the other couple aslo agreed to the price increase but they had not heard from them by then so that was obviously not a solution. They said that "we booked a tour that operates on cruise days", not the day before, and the conditions are stated on the website. If you check they never say this on the website. The company did not offer to refund the amount so, after many attempts (you can't reply to the Viator cancellation message or call directly), I finally got Viator to refund the tour but they offered no help to book an alternative transfer. review_text: We had an incredible experience with Sigrid Redlic, the daughter of the owner, Ervin. Sigrid speaks fluent English and was an informative guide. We chose the overnight option and were treated to a delicious full lunch at one farm and the hospitality of the hosts for a great dinner and experience of a local home farther up the lake for the night. With the new road going in, the traditional life of the people on Lago Espolin is changing. The trails they have ridden all their lives to get to their homes are no longer available. Ervin has developed new trails throughout his property which go through ancient forests, past waterfalls and have beautiful views of the lake. Some of these trails are quiet steep and technical, but the horses are sure footed. I don't know where the short ride would take you, but if you have time for a few hours, this experience is well worth it.

So if you would like to go to Torres del Paine please prepare your mind and specially keep walking! Torres's base route has a hard way in the end of way roughly for 3km always going up to the top of mountain where you can see the green lake. It's beautiful. It's amazing. It's unforgettable but you have to keep yourself strong and focused. Don't forget to bring water enough and food. You must be prepared. Important: In the low season, the Park only accepts Chilean cash. Dolar could be accepted in the high season but I'm not sure...just someone told me that.

review_text: Our cruise ship was making a nine-hour stop in Puerto Montt, and we wanted to see the local beauty. The ship offered excursions to the Petrowe River and the Osorno Volcano, but we knew that the efficiency of such excursions was very low. So we started looking for a private guide, with only two wishes: to see as many beauty as possible and avoid crowds of cruise passengers. Fortunately, we came across the website of the company "Roman Turventure" and agreed with Roman on this tour. Roman met us at the port, and the tour began. We went to the Osorno volcano to the level of the lower station of the chairlift, took this lift, then walked down to the car – the Weather God was kind to us, it was sunny and not windy, the beauty was over the roof! Then there is the quiet lake Todos los Santos ("lake of all saints"), the stormy and beautiful mountain river Petroue. The novel gave us a snack on the banks of this river, and showed us some little-known approaches to it - warm rounded rocks and blue-green water! Then we stopped by a llama farm and the final stop was the resort town of Puerto Varas on the shores of the serene Lake Llanquihue. The novel is incredibly energetic, sporty, social, knowing a lot about South America in general, and Chile in particular. Talking to him was one of the benefits of our tour. Great comfortable car, no rush - we always had the opportunity to linger and take pictures of anything we wanted. review_text: My partner and I were keen to see Antarctica but didn't relish a gut-retching two-day crossing of the Drake Passage. Antarctica XXI has solved this problem with a seamless fly-cruise experience. This is truly the best way to see Antarctica. We flew south early morning, arriving on King George Island in the South Shetlands less than two hours later. The flight was comfortable, using a modern STOL jet airliner. The crew on our boat were professional, attentive and clearly knew what they were doing. Each day's itinerary was packed with wildlife viewing and the scenery is breath-takingly pristine. You truly don't understand what "untouched by human hands" means until you visit Antarctica. It's also reassuring to know that the competing cruise companies share their planned itineraries at the start of the season, carefully mapping their routes and timing their arrival at each location so that you rarely see another vessel. We spent nine days at sea and saw a ship only three times and always in the distance. The wildlife is far more accessible and abundant than you'll ever believe. Our crew got us up close to a menagerie of animals very day. At least two, sometimes three, excursions were squeezed into every day including our arrival and departure days in the South Shetlands. Food on board was better than expected. A variety of dishes greeted us at every meal, presented simply but with taste and a hint of style. We also loved the small touches that made our cruise memorable. For example, guests were encouraged to share their best photos from the voyage. These were then added to a USB stick that every guest received on the final day. This stick also include detailed descriptions of our daily itinerary, along with maps and other background information. Antarctica XXI is also geared to handle the unexpected. Our luggage went missing between Santiago and Punta Arenas. LAN Chile gave us a number to call that was never answered and we began to despair that we'd have nothing to wear in Antarctica. However, the staff had contacts at the airline who were able to track down and deliver our luggage ten hours before our flight to Antarctica departed. We were also assured that the company had arrangements with a local retailer who'd open his doors at midnight if necessary to ensure we had suitable clothing no matter what happened. This is a small boat, staffed by a team that love their work. Spend a little extra and avoid the Drake Passage crossing. You won't be disappointed. Antarctica XXI delivers.

review_text: After all the horror stories I've heard of the San Pedro to Uyuni tour, I was wary of booking one. But my hostel I was staying at recommended this one and assured they offered a safe service, so I opted for it, and I'm glad I did! The tour with White and Green was extremely safe (which was my main concern), the drivers were professional and drove appropriately. Although they seemed a bit over worked and tired on the first day (they had to be up at 5am!) they managed to do the whole trip in a very safe manner! The trucks were also good, only had a small minor flat tire which was quickly fixed! The first night accommodation is COLD! Just like everywhere in the desert, bring many warm clothes and maybe a sleeping bag and you'll be fine! You also don't sleep above 4000m of altitude which is a good thing! The second night was in a Salt hotel and it was amazing! Warm and cozy, and wow what a place to look at the stars! (Again bring warm clothes for star gazing!) The food was really good, and plenty, always had enough for the big group of hungry travellers we were! If you (or someone in your group) speaks Spanish, it will help a lot! The drivers had a lot to say about the places were we visiting but only spoke Spanish! So if you speak Spanish a little bit, you'll get a driver AND a guide!! Overall, I'm happy I did it with White and green, the price was VERY cheap for the quality of the food and accommodation that you get! If I were to do it again, I would chose White and Green

review_text: Although it is possible to organize a tour of La Moneda on their website, it is somewhat complicated and requires a lot of information and advance planning. The vast majority will simply view the building from the south (Plaza de la Ciudadania) or the north (Plaza de la Constitucion). The building itself was the largest building in the Spanish Americas when it was completed in 1807 and it stately and unpretentious. The building's history as a mint, a presidential residence, the site of the 1973 coup, and as the executive office building is interesting. In the Plaza to the south you can visit the tomb of Bernardo O'Higgins on the rare occasions it is open to the public. In the Plaza to the north you can view the changing of the guard and a military band performance every other day. You can also see most of Chile's ministerial headquarters and the statues of famous presidents like Frei, Allende and Portales. Now there is a group food truck courtyard to the east of La Moneda and a great restaurant a block west called Blue Jar. Under La Moneda you can visit Centro Cultural La Moneda which has 3 excellent exhibitions per year. The area is a must visit although La Moneda itself is a bit underwhelming.

review_text: Of all the places we visited in and around Santiago, our trip to the Kingston Family Vineyards was the highlight. We learned about the history of the Kingston family and the historic changes in Chilean history/politics that ultimately allowed the family to maintain some of the best acreage in the valley for growing wine grapes. In fact, the commitment to maintain the family vineyards for future Kingston generations was so strong, it almost seemed like the family was there with us. We were treated to tastings outside in a charming stone alcove amid the vineyards, followed by a tour of the winery before enjoying a great dinner (with wines accompanying each course). It would be easy to say that the violinist that played at dinner was the most impressive part of the experience, but he played only second fiddle to the wine itself. They were fantastico. I particularly liked the refreshing Sauvignon Blanc we tasted first and a Pinot Noir we had at dinner. But all of the wines were very good. In total, the beautiful vineyards, winery, dinner and atmosphere made this the best wine touring experience I've ever had (including Napa, Bordeaux, Orvieto and Chianti). To reconnect with the experience, I'll probably either order some wines from their website or join their club where you're sent wines twice a year.

review_text: The tour was good with 14 people. The guide, Pablo, texted the night before on WhatsApp the time the bus would be picking us up and again a few minutes before arriving at the hotel. The driver was very good and the bus had the A/C on high so the 16 people on the bus did not get too hot. We stopped for just a few minutes at the the Rio Tinto Casablanca Restaurant to use the restrooms, get coffee, taste wine if you wanted to, and buy any souvenirs. Since the wine tasting was later in the day we did not buy wine here, but instead ordered a great Cortado (espresso with steamed milk). We went to Vina Del Mar and had a short stop at the Flower Clock, and then again a short stop near Playa Casino to view the beach. We then drove to Valparaiso, got out near the Ascensor Reina Victoria (funicular) and went up it to then do a short walking tour of the area before having lunch in La Casa Verde. The restaurant is really quite lovely with a few gift shops. The owner and servers are very friendly. We enjoyed the corn pie the best. review_text: The Yerba Loca Park is a great place to see an Andean valley near Santiago and to be able to do a hike that can be as long or as short as one wants. You will need a car to get to the park (on the road to Farellones ski resort). The park entrance where you register is right by the road and then there is a drive of 4 - 5 km up to the parking and camping areas. The path is clearly marked though can be a bit confusing at the start as there a multiple tracks. There are information posts that help identify the path and give information about the valley and its flora and fauna. The path steadily climbs from a start at 1950m and can be as long as 19km (one way to the terminal of the Paloma glacier (sadly in retreat) at 4000m. There are steeper parts of the path than others, but it is nice at the end of the day's trekking that it is all downhill. Cerro Altar, Cer Manchon, Cerro Altar Falso, Cerro La Paloma, all peaks in excess of 4000m are visible during the hike. Take a picnic, sunblock and plenty of water (especially in summer) as the main stream has high content of salts that make it undrinkable. There is camping at Villa Paulina, the start of the trek as well as camping places along the trail (pack in what you need).

review_text: We werent brave enough to do the full W so we did a 1 day hike up to Torres, then the west V staying at the refugio Paine Grande. Day hike Torres - the bus is 15,000 pp return which our hostel booked for us. It picked us up from our hostel between 730-8am. It takes 2 hrs but you stop half way at a shop/cafe for a 10/15 minute break. They have a few snacks if you need to beef up your food supplies but nothing substantial. The bus drops you at Amarga, where you sign into the park, pay 18,000 pp park entry fee and watch an introductory video. From here you either get back on the bus to Pudeto (catamaran port) or administracion, or you can get a shuttle to Hosteria Las Torres (the start of the Torres/w Trek) or you can start walking from here. We didnt have enough cash for the shuttle so started walking - note that its 7.5km to the hosteria Las Torres which is meant to take 2.5 hrs. We started hiking at 10.30 as soon as we got into the park and got back to the park entrance at 7.30 just in time for the last bus at 7.45 - we had to walk at a very fast pace and had to jog part of the last stretch as we were cutting it close. If you are doing a day trek to torres i would strongly suggest taking the shuttle at least one way to give yourself a few extra hours on the hike and time to get back for the bus. As for the hike, its a steady incline pretty much the whole way. its really not too bad until the last 45 mins up to the viewpoint. The last section is horrendously steep and a tough trek but definitely worth it. It was snowing, windy and bitterly cold when we got to the top but the laguna is stunning and we got a glimpse of the towers which made it all worthwhile. West V - Your park entry lasts for 3 days, so as we returned within that time frame we didnt have to pay again. We got the bus into the park, arrived at amarga at 10. We stayed on the bus whilst everyone else checked in and paid. We then continued on the bus to Pudeto, arriving at about 11. There is a small cafe you can wait in until the ferry goes at 12. You buy your tickets (12,000 pp) on the boat and they check your tickets as you get off. The boat ride is only 30 minutes across the beautiful blue lago pehoe - definitely go onto the roof of the boat to get some scenic piccies. Once arrived at Paine Grande, we checked into our dorm and headed up to Glacier Grey. This hike is a gradual incline to the mirador - 1.5 hrs in - which gives you a fantastic view of the glacier. If you dont have time to do the full Grey trek, definitely make time to get to the mirador. Its stunning. After here, its another 2 hrs (more rocky and steeper inclines/declines) to the camp and then after the camp another 30 mins to the viewpoint. Its a nice glacier but if you have seen Perito Moreno you wont be WOWed by this one. At Paine Grande Refugio, dinner is $20 pp, 3 course meal from 7-9. I had read terrible reviews about the food but was actually quite impressed. Its really not that bad. There is a little bar above the cafeteria if you fancy a post hike nightcap. Our dorm was 6 beds - 47$ per night with no food or blankets included - shared bathrooms. Its expensive but there arent too many other options if you dont want to camp! The dorms were nice but ours was very cold so you might need some extra layers! On the 2nd day we attempted the Frances Valley trek. The trek to Camp Italiano is a nice scenic walk, not too challenging and has some fantastic views. By the time we got to the camp the heavens had opened, the rain was falling hard and our desire to climb any further disappeared, so we took the lazy option and headed back for the earlier ferry (12.30). I have a lot of respect for all those that do the full W, its a tough trek, much harder than El Chalten, and the weather was on off rain/wind/cold so you are often trekking your heart out for no view but hopefully the sense of achievement and experience makes it all worthwhile!

review_text_preprocessed: We werent brave enough to do the full W so we did a 1 day hike up to Torres, then the west V staying at the refugio Paine Grande. Day hike Torres - the bus is 15,000 pp return which our hostel booked for us. It picked us up from our hostel between 730-8am. It takes 2 hrs but you stop half way at a shop/cafe for a 10/15 minute break. They have a few snacks if you need to beef up your food supplies but nothing substantial. The bus drops you at Amarga, where you sign into the park, pay 18,000 pp park entry fee and watch an introductory video. From here you either get back on the bus to Pudeto (catamaran port) or administracion, or you can get a shuttle to Hosteria Las Torres (the start of the Torres/w Trek) or you can start walking from here. We didnt have enough cash for the shuttle so started walking - note that its 7.5km to the hosteria Las Torres which is meant to take 2.5 hrs. We started hiking at 10.30 as soon as we got into the park and got back to the park entrance at 7.30 just in time for the last bus at 7.45 - we had to walk at a very fast pace and had to jog part of the last stretch as we were cutting it close. If you are doing a day trek to torres i would strongly suggest taking the shuttle at least one way to give yourself a few extra hours on the hike and time to get back for the bus. As for the hike, its a steady incline pretty much the whole way. its really not too bad until the last 45 mins up to the viewpoint. The last section is horrendously steep and a tough trek but definitely worth it. It was snowing, windy and bitterly cold when we got to the top but the laguna is stunning and we got a glimpse of the towers which made it all worthwhile. West V - Your park entry lasts for 3 days, so as we returned within that time frame we didnt have to pay again. We got the bus into the park, arrived at amarga at 10. We stayed on the bus whilst everyone else checked in and paid. We then continued on the bus to Pudeto, arriving at about 11. There is a small cafe you can wait in until the ferry goes at 12. You buy your tickets (12,000 pp) on the boat and they check your tickets as you get off. The boat ride is only 30 minutes across the beautiful blue lago pehoe - definitely go onto the roof of the boat to get some scenic piccies. Once arrived at Paine Grande, we checked into our dorm and headed up to Glacier Grey. This hike is a gradual incline to the mirador - 1.5 hrs in - which gives you a fantastic view of the glacier. I had read terrible reviews about the food but was actually quite impressed. Its really not that bad. There is a little bar above the cafeteria if you fancy a post hike nightcap. Our dorm was 6 beds - 47$ per night with no food or blankets included - shared bathrooms. Its expensive but there arent too many other options if you dont want to camp! The dorms were nice but ours was very cold so you might need some extra layers! On the 2nd day we attempted the Frances Valley trek. review_text: The Cathedral in Santiago's Plaza de Armas is a great building, the kind of 'classical' cathedral of the late XVIII you find in many western cities, including southAmerican capitals. It shows the might and power of the Spanish and Portuguese catholic conquerors, and it truly deserves a visit. It always makes an impressive change coming from the noisy environment you find downtown, into this huge gallery. If you happen to enter during the mass, then the effect is even better with voices and chants echoing inside. The Cathedral sits in the main Plaza, built over the former Inca shrine, not far from the river and looking to a 5400 meter high mountain - today mostly hidden by the high rises - from where the sun shines on the summer solstice.

review_text: We met our tour leader/driver, Jorge Naveas (lacitroverde@gmail.com) and his associate, Javiera Uribe as we walked through the Coquimbo cruise port gate. Our first stop was El Faro (Lighthouse) in La Serena before heading East along the river valley. Next stop was the Puclaro Dam and beautiful reservoir. Traveling through many vineyards we arrived in the picturesque town of Vicuna, the birthplace of Literary Nobel Prize-winner Gabriela Mistral. Local sights included her museum/home, a beautiful main square, and the Bauer Tower. The next stop was Pisquera Aba, a distillery for Pisco, the national drink of Chile... that's what all of the grapes are used for !!! An interesting tour and free samples! Before our return to Coquimbo a stop was made for home-made sweet treats. This was a wonderful private tour in a vintage vehicle, and a definite highlight in our 32 day cruise!!! We appreciate your honest evaluation of your experience, with joy and knowledge are always welcome Mrs. Patricia and husband. see you soon Jorge Naveas Bravo La Citro Verde lacitroverde@gmail.com

review_text: After reading SEVERAL horror stories about transportation in general in Chile, I was very scared and skeptical, but after finding one person who had a positive experience with this company, I decided to go with the TransVIP company. I did not pay for it online, even though this is an option, but rather, planned to make my reservation at the airport in case it was a scam. It was not at all!! (How relieving!) There was an available TransVIP desk at the exit of the airport (along with a bunch of other transportation companies too). The vans are small, (7 seats) and there are plenty available. They filled up in a few seconds and we were off! (We went from Calama Airport to San Pedro de Atacama and back). If you book at the desk, they offer you a small discount for scheduling the roundtrip ticket instead of two one-way tickets. On the way back, they picked us up on time, in our planned on hotel spot and again, NO ISSUES AT ALL. The van only had my husband and I, and 2 other girls. Another review that I read was that the vans had to be completely full in order to run, and this was not the case. The driver was really nice too. My husband actually lost his cell phone, and once we realized this, the driver let us make phone calls on his personal cell to our previous hotel/tour company to try to track it down. He even pulled over on the side of the road, in case we wanted to turn around, but we would have missed our flight, so we did not turn around to go get the phone. I would recommend TransVIP and definitely use them again and recommend them to anyone without any hesitations. The prices are posted, receipts are given with times and locations of pickups, and it is a very straightforward, easy and seamless experience.

review_text: If you are researching the W trek and what to book, look no further.. just contact Ricci and the crew at Chiletour and you will be sorted for everything. It was a dream finding this company as I was unsure of where to go first, what to book etc. After emailing Chiletour they were so friendly and helpful, didn't need to worry about a thing after, just showed up. Arrived into Puerto Natales airport on day 1 where they were waiting for us with our name on a little sign as we arrived 😃 private transfer with Carrie to Ricci's place for our intro. They made us feel right at home as soon as we walked through the door. Sat us down with some lovely fresh brown bread, jams and cheeses and wine! Gave us a little pack with all our accomodation, transfer tickets, maps and itinerary all ready to go. Went through a presentation and through the park in detail and answered all our questions. After checking into our room for the night, they then brought us out to a local bar where we all had more wine, delicious pizza and a great chat, which was all included in the deal! After a great nights rest and breakfast, oh and our yummy packed lunch prepared by Ricci, we were back into the private transfer to the national park. We had a guide for the day, Ian, who was very experienced and knowledgable of the park and the trek. He kept an eye on everyone throughout the day trip and was good fun also. He got us all to the top of Mirador del Torres and back again safely. Every day after that for the rest of the W we were by ourselves and I think that was perfect for us. It was nice to have a guide on the first day to help get aquatinted with the park and then to work your own way through the rest of the trek was no trouble at all. Each of the check ins were hassle free and we were also checked as full board so we had breakfast, dinner and a box lunch prepared each day before our trek. We also decided last minute to do a glacier walk which Ricci organise for us while we were busy trekking. He sent all the details of the booking to one of the Refugios who printed it out for us- so helpful! He was always available when we needed him. At the end of the whole tour we were shattered! Finally made it back to get the boat across lake pehoe where we met our bus driver to take us back to Puerto Natales. It was such a relief to get back home to Riccis which was late at that stage. Again greeted with open arms and welcome home drinks 😄 we were just too tired to have any!! We settled into our cosy beds for the night! The following morning Ricci had a lovely home cooked breaky for us which was just perfecto 👌after our final chats and goodbyes, he dropped us up to the bus station to make sure we got on our bus and on our way. I recommend Ricci and the Chiletour team 100%. The detail, care and customer service was outstanding. I felt like we were visiting friends more than a tour company. If you are unsure of who to do the tour with or how to book, look no further!! Thanks again guys for the amazing experience 👍 Thank you so much for a very detailed reflection of your experience here in Patagonia. Come again.

review_text: A scenic commentary was provided in all public areas of the ship. Cape Horn marks the northern boundary of the Drake Passage, the body of water between South America's Cape Horn: the southwestern part of the Atlantic Ocean with the southeastern part of the Pacific Ocean and extends into the Southern Ocean. Cape Horn is half-way between Australia and England. The passage, named after the English explorer and privateer Sir Francis Drake, is considered one of the most treacherous voyages for ships to make. Its strong winds, large waves, and currents caused many sailors get lost, delayed, and perished in these waters. There is a monument that sits atop Cape Horn. It is a large silhouette of an Albatross in honor of the sailors who died while attempting to go around Cape Horn. The Chilean navy has a permanent lighthouse on the island (with a resident lighthouse keeper), as well as a small Chapel. From a distance (unless you had a large lens), we saw the lightkeeper's house and the memorial to lost sailors. We learned in this area there are some 800 ships lying beneath these waters which drop from some 300 feet to thousands of feet in just a short distance. In 1905, about 130 ships attempted the transition from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and some 50 were unaccounted for. It was the record year for such tragedies.

review_text: I've studied human rights for years, so my opinion may be a bit biased, but I strongly recommend visiting this museum regardless of your background knowledge of Chile (actually, especially if you know nothing about it), your political leanings, or schedule while in Santiago. The Andes, the cerros downtown, and the vineyards are all important to see while in Santiago, but to really understand Chilean culture and society, this museum is the place to go. The museum presents human rights and the Pinochet dictatorship in a very easy to understand way, mixes presentations with interactive material, and is very easy to stroll through at your own pace. If you need a moment to regroup or just take a break from all the information you're absorbing, there's a quiet cafe on the top floor, along with a gallery that always has new installations. From an aesthetic standpoint, this is by far the best museum in Santiago.

review_text: We chose White & Green as we wanted to have an English speaking guide. Booking through white & green means that you get a driver and a separate guide. A lot of companies might say that they can provide an English speaking guide but this is often just the driver. Some people say that it is a visual tour so you don’t need any explanation but we found it incredibly helpful having an English speaking guide so that we could ask questions at all the stops but also throughout each day which meant we really got to learn more about Bolivia and the salt flats. Our driver was Freddy and our guide was Omar. They were brilliant. Freddy was such a safe driver and Omar went out of his way to be helpful especially on the last day taking all the salt flats pictures for us. Hostels were basic but because it was quiet m, our group all got separate rooms. You had to pay for hot showers and I found that even when paying sometimes they weren’t hot so beware. Food was plentiful, maybe not as great if you are vegetarian but they certainly tried to accommodate. They also let you know when there are stops to buy snacks etc. Would thoroughly recommend white & green. They were really professional and we came away feeling like we had learnt a lot.

review_text: During our trip to Chile, my wife and I had the incredible opportunity to visit natural hot springs, and it was an invigorating and unforgettable experience that combined natural beauty with a feeling of deep relaxation. Natural Wonder: Chile's hot springs are true natural wonders. These pools of hot water emerge from underground, heated by volcanic activity. Hot water springs from the depths of the volcanoes and joins the porous rocks, creating a unique and fascinating scene. This natural movement causes an effect similar to that of a pressure cooker, resulting in a thermal bath experience that is both exhilarating and relaxing. Stunning Scenery: Hot springs are situated in stunning landscapes, often surrounded by mountains and lush vegetation. The contrast between the warm waters and the fresh mountain air creates a magical atmosphere. The rock formations around the pools add a rustic, natural feel, making you feel truly immersed in nature. Each hot spring offers spectacular views that contribute to the feeling of tranquility and well-being. Relaxing Effect: Soaking in the hot waters of the hot springs was an incredibly relaxing experience. The water temperature is perfect for relieving muscle tension and providing a feeling of comfort and relaxation. We spent hours enjoying the different pools, each with its own temperature and characteristics. It was wonderful to feel the warm, bubbling water all around us, while hearing the soothing sounds of nature all around us. Health Benefits: In addition to relaxation, hot springs are known for their therapeutic benefits. Mineral-rich waters help improve circulation, relieve muscle and joint pain and promote a general feeling of well-being. We left the pools feeling refreshed and energized, ready to continue exploring the beauty of Chile. Access and Structure: The hot springs are well-maintained and accessible, with well-equipped changing and rest areas. The facilities are clean and well maintained, ensuring a comfortable experience for all visitors. The staff on site were friendly and helpful, providing information about the properties of the waters and ensuring our visit was enjoyable. In summary: Our experience at Chile's hot springs was unforgettable. The combination of stunning scenery, warm, relaxing waters and health benefits made this activity one of the highlights of our trip. We highly recommend everyone to visit these natural wonders for an experience of deep relaxation and connection with nature. Chile's hot springs are a hidden gem that provide moments of peace and revitalization. Review of: Volcano & Hotsprings 4K

review_text: Its pretty cool. I mean how often do you find a flower clock, really?? Take a cab because its a bit of a traffic issue getting there. Once there you can walk back to town but it will take you about 45 minutes. This attraction is practically, directly across from the Sheraton Hotel which is probably the nicest place to stay in the Vina area. To give you a bit more of a background on Vina Del Mar; My wife, 11 year old daughter and I ventured onward to Vina Del Mar and Renaca, Chile this past Christmas vacation of 2013. Due to rave reviews from friends/expats in the US, we have been talking about visiting here for quite a while. We were sorely underwhelmed by this place in the world, to say the least. Let me begin by asking your reasons for wanting to visit the Vina del Mar area? If you have to go for business and the company is picking up the tab, well okay. There are worse places. If you are going to discover new culture, fine architecture, great beaches and interesting people, there are 1,000 better places. If you are from the US and taking a family vacation here, willingly, I would ask you to make an appointment with a neurologist. There is nothing about Vina Del Mar, nor Renaca, that even remotely has an edge over the most basic of budget beach resorts at the Jersey Shore. All the beaches, in and around this area from Vina Del Mar all the way up and through Renaca AND beyond, are dumpy, dingy and dirty. Many as well reek of urine, either from the horse drawn carriages, stray dogs or homeless people in and around the area. They're just NOT at all pretty. You walk out on the rocks on the beach at Renaca and find trash and more urine smell, at one time so pungent I nearly vomited. Want to go swimming? We were there on the first day of summer, Dec 21, and it was pretty cold just to walk around. But even in the height of their short summer months, January and February, the water remains Ice-Cap bitter cold due to the area's proximity to the Antarctic. Beware as well that Vina Del Mar has both a homeless problem, and an incredibly LARGE stray dog issue. The dogs are all nice and appear to be well fed, but they are literally everywhere; street corners, main roads and especially on the beach. If you're a dog person you'll love it because they are all very cute and people friendly. But, they are dogs, and do what dogs do. Some early mornings you are woken by their territorial stampede as rivaling packs fight for dominance before the traffic gets too bad. They then calm down until the next sunrise. This is NOT a family vacation destination, especially if you have US teens. Understand that Vina Del Mar is VERY third world, and certainly not the mecca of art, culture and beach swimming it is touted to be by people trying to sell you something. The restaurants are mediocre to good, but in some areas downright awful. There are 2 Starbucks in Vina thank God. You can not get a decent cup of Joe anywhere in this God forsaken country. We ordered a very mediocre lunch in a "café" on Liberdad (one of the main drags) with some Café con Leche. The waiter arrived with instant coffee, a pot of hot water and 2 milk cartons.......and if that wasn't comical enough, one afternoon we ordered omelettes and a cheese sandwich. We all received ham and "cheese of the day" sandwiches and the waiter ran away after placing them on our table. Yes, I do speak pretty good Spanish and ordered correctly, this is just an extremely odd country, and that being said, there is more................ A man came up to us as we were walking to dinner one night down 5 Norte, waving his hands at me as he got closer. Each hand contained a large nail. He was insisting I listen to something which sounded like the beginning of a zealous, inspired personal discourse on the death of Christ, and he waved the nails in my face for a moment before we all walked off. It took us a little while after some laughter to try and figure out what he was attempting to say. Did he want to sell us the nails for 1000 pesos? Why not? Various people walk around selling random band-aids, so why not nails? Perhaps he wanted a hammer? Help putting up some new shelving in his home? Nope, it was probably about some religious fanaticism, which breeds a somewhat puritanical and conservative air to the place. My 11 year old daughter wore typical US teen tights and a t-shirt one afternoon and the doorman stopped me, saying she was dressed inappropriately and requested she change. Whattttt?????!!! The same doorman hassled a younger woman for entering the building, wearing a skirt on the short side with boots. This, as an American, I found most bizarre. In a nutshell, we were in Vina Del Mar as an American family for 8 days, and it was 8 days too long. It is old, smelly, and dumpy, lacking in character. One post I read before arriving there compared Vina Del Mar to Barcelona. What a farce! Barcelona is a beautiful European city and Vina Del Mar is a dump; an armpit comparatively to Barcelona. Don't waste your time traveling to Vina Del Mar, nor its neighboring towns like Valparaiso or Renaca, which are even dumpier. Valparaiso is so old, decrepit and run down it looks like a hellish version of San Francisco in 1960 during a garbage pick up strike.

review_text: I took this hike for the first time on a Monday about Midday. The road way up to the top had relatively few cars, and not very many people. The walk up from the front gates took about 45 minutes with stops for photos along the way. The walk is fairly straight forward and very easy. When I got to the top, it was incredibly peaceful, even though they had hymns playing over the PA system, that I am assuming they use when they have services. They were probably 10-15 people at the top with me and we all just sat in silence just admiring the view and enjoying the peace and quiet away from Santiago’s hustle and bustle. I took a second trip up to the statue with a friend for a Saturday night sunset and it was considerably busier. The views of the sunset were nice but it was less peaceful as there were LOTS of people there. I was a little worried about the walk down not knowing if the pathway was lit, but for the most part it was and hassle free as there were plenty of other people there walking back as well. The sunset was good and I got some ok photos but I had a much nicer experience mid week when it was amazingly peaceful and plenty of opportunity to take uninterrupted photos of the vast Santiago skyline. (The first trip up was the first day of my holidays so maybe I was just incredibly happy to be out of the office ☺).

review_text: We had done the standard "see the city" bus tour and a great deal of wandering about on our own. But this morning we went on the free walking tour called "Offbeat Santiago" to see another side of the city. And our guide Ignacio more than fulfilled the website's promise. We saw markets and side streets we did not even know existed, learned about traditional foods and where to get them, and toured the major cemetery. Interspersed with history, explanations of social classes in Chile, food and drink descriptions, and a very personal but even handed political history lesson were answers to any offbeat question any one wanted to ask (for example: what is with all the dogs, who all seem friendly but are not wearing collars and seem to be moving freely about the city?) Go on the tour and ask to find out! Ignacio spoke great English and was just generally an incredible guide -- by the end of the tour we wanted to give him our contact information and tell him to contact us if he ever made it to our area. He was personable but the tour was not about him -- that aspect just brought it to life. His love of Santiago and of Chile shone through the whole tour. All in all, it was the best part of our visit. We will soon be in Valparaiso and will check out the same group there because we had such a good time today. HE provided a general guideline re the average tip they are given -- I would be stunned if any but students on a strict budget did not double or triple that modest amount -- the tour was worth far more. Do wear very comfortable walking shoes, a hat and sunscreen and some drinking water -- it was hot and involved time in the sun, although Ignacio did his talking with us in the shade even if he was in full sun.

review_text: The place is absolutely beautiful and there are plenty of places to lounge and relax while drinking a coffee or waiting for your tour to start. Unfortunately, the service in the restaurant is quite inattentive. It took half an hour for a waiter to show up to bring us a menu when there were very few people in the restaurant (we wanted a coffee while we were waiting for our friend's tour to start). The tasting by itself wasn't very informative, but for CH$9.500 the wine was good and I liked how we were able to do the premium tasting while our friends who took the basic tour got their basic tasting at the same time. Some people might not like that, but I thought it was great! (granted, this might be why it wasn't very informative trying to explain both the Reserve and Grand Reserve of the same variety at the same time.) We had the same waiter for lunch and it took over an hour between ordering and for the meals to arrive, with several tables that ordered similar meals next to us getting their appetizers and meals, despite ordering after us. There was zero explanation of why it was taking so long, and he didn't even bother to bring a second round of mini-sopaipillas/bread until made a comment to the hostess around the 50 minute mark (I actually checked my timestamp from taking pictures of the cute mini-sopaipillas). When the food arrived it was all delicious. I tried my fiance's spare ribs and polenta/grits and I ordered a soup and split a (very tasty and filling) salad with a friend. But, again when we ordered a salad to split between two people and he brought two plates, no extra utensils were brought to serve the salad. A small detail, but they add up. We then decided to order dessert! I would definitely pass on this if I went back. The creme brulee didn't have a crunch, and the "cheesecake" was essentially vanilla yogurt, cookie crumbs, and chocolate chips in a mini-jar. It also took a half an hour for the desert to arrive after ordering (maybe this is why the brulee no longer crunched?) It's a shame because I heard such great things about the restaurant, and the main meals were delicious, but the service was seriously lacking.

review_text: We spent 4 days touring The Atacama on long day trips from San Pedro with Jorge Jerez in October. Jorge knows the area intimately, including many hidden corners, which were invariably the highlights. Importantly, he was resourceful and reprogrammed our whole itinerary when we were delayed 36 hours leaving Santiago during the recent protests and again when the town ran out of fuel! The most amazing day was mostly spent off-road in the National Reserve Los Flamencos and at Sala de Tara (Flamingoes galore) - unworldly Rock formations and a wow moment around every bend. Vicuña everywhere too. We also visited Tatio Geysers - reputedly the areas top attraction. To us it was an expensive disappointment; it may be the highest geothermal field in an amazing landscape, but the geysers themselves were not anywhere near as spectacular as we’d seen in Iceland. We stayed at the Ckoi Hotel just 5 minutes walk into the old town with many good local places to eat - recommend Adobe and Las Delicias de Carmen - for good tourist 3 star accommodation. You will return with great memories of landscapes and wildlife. Thank you very much! I am sorry about the geysers....

review_text: After walking up and down the streets of San Pedro trying to choose an agency - we decided to go with a White and Green because they offered an English speaking guide (1 of 2 that we found, the other is World White Travel). We paid $150CLP each for the 3 days which included all meals and accommodation, driver and guide. (Note- you have to pay 10 Bolivianos for hot water showers at the both of the hostels and also 3-5 Bolivianos for most of the toilets along the way as well as national park entry fees. And if you want/are told you are getting a private room, make sure it’s written on your tour voucher!) Our driver was Elmer who navigated the difficult terrain with ease. We felt completely safe. Our guide was Marcelo who was very keen to give us a A LOT of information about the different places and sites which is fine but he was a little pushy at times with the information kind of forcing it on us and asking us to ask him questions even if we didn’t have any. Sometimes just being silent and taking in the new surroundings is enough for some people. This time of year is extremely cold and while we were warned we weren’t really warned about the icy cold winds as well, we could have better prepared our clothing for the first day if we had known. The food was quite good. If you are a vegetarian make sure you bring extra snacks because you will mostly be fed omelettes and eggs plus the vegetables, salad and soups that everyone else gets. Another note is that our guide was chewing coca leaves the whole time, we have no problem with that except for the fact it can be quite pungent when you are stuck in the car with no A/C and not able to open the windows because of the dust. Im sure other guides/drivers chew it too but it’s just something to note if you are sensitive to smells. All in all it was a hectic few days but can definitely recommend for a memorable experience.

review_text: We caught the Ho-Ho at the large shopping / eating mall on Avienda Kennedy (just up the road from our hotel). We found it a good idea to get off at the city centre and explore on foot, then made our way back to the same stop to see some of the bits we had missed. It's definitely best to sit upstairs as the views are very restricted downstairs. Maps and earphones are provided with interesting commentary in several languages. A one day ticket cost 21,000 Pesos (around £20) and was excellent value for money and a great way to see a beautiful city. Well worth it! Thank you for your comment! Overall totally amazing!

review_text: Using the tower as a land mark, I had no problems finding the mall, but the actual elevator for the tower was a problem, but after I found it Maria was the first person I saw. She took a group of tourist up to the top of the deck; she then asked where everyone was from, I was the only American. She explained that she will do a tour in one language (french I believe) and another person did one in spanish. As I was the only english speaker I was kind of left to fend for myself. I quickly noticed the floor of the deck had circles with different names, and is you stand on them you can hear an audio message; every so often the language of the message would change. After figuring that out I went to each circle and listened to what the message said. There aren't many markers to point out what some of the messages spoke about., but I did my best to guess which building or area the speaker was giving insight into. After I was done with the messages and about to leave, Maria stopped me. She said she was looking for me to give me an english tour. I was shocked and promptly said yes. She asked for 5 mins to see if she could find any other english speakers to give the tour to. A few moments later she found me with 2 Chilean men who spoke a little english, they decided to work on their english by listening to the tour. She then took me around and explained every significant spot we could see. I was quite impressed with the control of the english language. If you go, ask for Maria, she was help full with tips for, night time activities, the local eateries, beers, and parks. I really appreciated her taking the time to look for me and do a tour pretty much for me.

review_text: We were driven in a minibus from La Serena with 11 other guests. Our guide was bilingual - he easily slipped from Spanish to English and vice versa. Being an ex primary school teacher, he had the gift of the teacher and made the day most enjoyable. We stopped at various points to have items of interest pointed out to us. The papaya shop was the first proper stop, followed by the dam. This poor dam is down to 3% of its water quantity but it was great to see the valley and the river. The Pisco producing place was astonishing: everything was still done by hand, including filling the bottles and corking them up. Lunch in the hotel Elqui was good and the visit to the Gabriella Mistral museum was fascinating. The Elqui valley is very beautiful and definitely worth a trip. It's nice to know where those delicious avocados are grown!

review_text: Because of the high recommendations given to Jaime of PatagoniaShorex Tours on Trip Advisor and Cruise Critic, I contacted him to organise a 4 day deviation tour for 18 passengers who were travelling on the Sea Princess World Cruise, to visit Cusco, Lima, Sacred Valley, Ollantaytambo, Aquas Calientes and Machu Picchu. He was patient with those who needed extra help, and it just got better and better as we made our way to the highlight of the trip, Machu Picchu. Most meals were included and he arranged excellent accommodation, especially The El Mapi hotel in Aguas Calientes. It was a two minute walk to catch the bus for the 20 minute ride up the mountain to Machu Picchu, and we were able to be on the site before it became very crowded later in the morning. A tour with Jaime in this part of the world is an 'absolute must' for anyone who has the opportunity to do it, it is important to deal with someone who knows the area and is able to structure a tour to include as much as possible in the time you have, and do it for a price and standard you require. review_text: We had six free days to fill while in the Santiago area. What to do? A web search stumbled upon the “Chile Wine Experience 6D Tour” offered by Ecotours. After some initial hesitation (Could we survive a six day wine tour? Ouch, the price! Do we dare do a wire transfer to someone we don't know on the other side of the Equator?), we decided to jump in. Ecotour's great reviews on TripAdvisor gave us some peace of mind. It turned out to be one of traveling's great experiences. The day-by-day tour details can be found on Ecotour's website. While on initial reading, that write-up sounds a bit “fluffy”, it turned out to be spot on with our actual experience. Our driver Ricardo was more than just a “driver” - he seemed to know everyone, everywhere, and handled much of the travel logistics. Our guide Javier was a walking encyclopedia of Chilean history/geography/society/politics/vinology, with a wickedly funny sense of humor. They kept us easily entertained for all six days. Seamlessly behind the curtain, Cristian was making sure that all went smoothly. We threw some initial sand into the gears when our flight out of Easter Island to Santiago took a multiple bird strike into the left engine upon take-off (my first aborted take-off), and we had to return to Easter Island. So we were delayed 12 hours. Nevertheless, when our replacement 767 arrived at Santiago, there were Ricardo and Javier at the airport, waiting to collect us. The wine tour was more than just a seemingly endless string of wine tastings. The Chilean wineries provided a diverse collection of fascinating, culturally authentic architectures – not the faux chateaux of Napa. We also visited two superb museums as part of the tour: the Museo Andino at Santa Rita and the Colchagua Museum in Santa Cruz. At the top of the lodgings experience was La Casona on the grounds of Matetic Vineyards: a 7-room boutique hotel in a century old colonial style. And all the marvelous, wine-paired meals during the week – oh, my! The pacing during the tour was just right, not too fast, not too slow. The climax was, of course, the visit to Lapostolle in the Apalta Valley (the apex of Chilean wines) on the final day (clue: the founder's middle name is Marnier, as in Grand...). Their production facility looks like a set from a James Bond thriller. The lunch on their restaurant porch overlooking the Valley was THE highpoint of the tour. It helps that Lapostolle is one of only two establishments in all of Chile in the Relais & Chateaux collection. Talk about finishing on a high point! Altogether, we spent four weeks in Chile. Ecotour's six day wine tour cemented our impressions: we love Chile!

review_text: I did a weekend-long guided whitewater trip down Rio San Pedro with Kayak Chile and it was absolutely incredible!!! The rapids themselves were amazing..the first day is a good warm up for the bigger rapids in the morning on the second day. review_text: Thank you, Atacama Experience, for the most wonderful trip to Atacama and Uyuni. The scenery of these places was unimaginably beautiful and I was glad to have joined a private tour with Paola as our guide and Richie/Edgar as our driver. I’m still thinking about the trip. Right from the beginning, David (Atacama logistic) was extremely helpful and prompt in answering my multiple and repetitive questions. He provided valuable suggestions to help customise my personalised 12 days itinerary. Apart from being greeted with astonishing scenery, the pace of our tour was comfortable as the itinerary was adjusted to meet our physical capabilities. When we did the long uphill walks with Paolo, she was mindful to set a slow pace and we took short breaks every 15min. She was even kind enough to offer to carry our water bottles. During times when we were too tired to walk, Richie/Edgar drove us close to the sites so we can view and take pictures from the car. They were very accommodating to our needs and even went to find suitable private toilet for us, when possible. During our conversations, I made a passing remark that I’m scared of the wind and my travel companion is scared of the sunshine. I was pleased and surprised that our guide had taken this into consideration when setting up our outdoor lunch. Where possible, Paola searched for areas which sheltered us from the sun or wind so that we can have a pleasant meal in front of the spectacular views. I was very delighted to have the chance to eat my lunch facing the Talar Salt Flats with no wind in my face and eating in the Uyuni salt flats with a rented umbrella over our heads. Towards the end of one of my day tour, I experienced a bit of altitude sickness. The next day, the Paola/Richie brought me an insulated bottle of coca leaf tea. It tasted nice and I thought this was a lovely gesture. Paola has extensive knowledge of flora, fauna, marine, geology, astronomy, etc, you can pretty much ask her anything and she will be happy to share her knowledge and travels with you. She is environmentally conscious as I heard her telling other tourist many times to respect the protective boundaries of the sites. This is a great asset as it would be a big shame for the stunning scenery of Atacama to be polluted and ruined by people who are not respectful of nature. Anyone thinking about going to Atacama should definitely book a private tour with Atacama Experience. It had enriched my experience and I want to visit again!

review_text: This was the trip of a lifetime for many reasons. I won't focus on the specifics of our experience (which were amazing) because we got really lucky with weather and other factors. Below I will list the systematic aspects of Yak Expediciones that ensure you will have the trip of a lifetime regardless of the weather conditions. First, this region is absolutely beautiful in any weather. It was such a treat to get to paddle down these fjords. Second, Juanfe is a GREAT guide. Most importantly, he has decades of experience, is highly competent and safety oriented, and has a network of fishing families in the area. My fiance and I both felt very safe with him. He is very skilled at teaching and managing the group to help you get your most out of your experience. Sometimes that means getting you to paddle harder, sometimes that means goofing around having fun with you. Usually it means giving you chocolate to keep you going! Third, it was a great bonding experience with the rest of the group. On a trip like this you get really close with the other members of the group. Fourth, the families we stayed at were so kind and welcoming. And they provided lots and lots of delicious local seafood. Fifth, the physical challenge and learning was satisfying. This trip was physically challenge despite my fiance and I being in very good condition. However, Juanfe was very supportive and helped us improve our technique. By the end of the trip we had both improved considerably in our kayaking skills. This trip is absolutely worth the price and the time to get down here. Thanks Juanfe for such a great experience. Nos vemos en el agua!

review_text: Tour guide Denis Purtov was great! A very comprehensive tour for the cost, the group (in a van holding 10 people very comfortably) first hit a few highlights in the industrial city of Peurto Montt, then headed out of town on a beautifully clear day. After awhile we started seeing the snow-capped peak of Volcano Osorno, and stopped to take pictures of it overlooking the beautiful Lake Llanquihue at a small llama farm. The llamas delighted everyone with their antics. We shortly moved on to our next stop at beautiful Petrohue Falls (Vincent Perez Rosales National Park, admission extra $6USD) with its many scenic vistas. There were some handicraft markets near the gate as well, with alpaca sweaters, scarves, and so forth. We moved on to view the peaceful Green Lagoon (colored dramatically by algae) and hiked on in a short distance to view beautiful Lake Llanquihue. Since the potentially fickle weather remained calm and clear for us, we then headed up towards the peak of Volcano Osorno on the twisty mountainous road to a height of about 8,700 feet, where the ski lift started (which was operating but which we did not take.) review_text: The San Francisco Church is a Franciscan church on Avenida Libertador General Bernardo O'Higgins in downtown of Santiago. The church, along with the adjacent convent, is one of the oldest colonial-era buildings in Chile and the oldest one in Santiago. The church was consecrated in 1622. It’s bell tower was destroyed by an earthquake in 1647, while the rest of the building successfully resisted it. In 1730 another earthquake badly damaged the rebuilt tower, which was demolished in 1751. The current bell tower is of Victorian architecture and was constructed in the mid-1800s. It’s architect was Fermín Vivaceta and features a distinctive clock. Could not visit inside. Certainly would very highly recommend visiting this old church.

review_text: We stayed at this beautiful hotel and winery for 4 days- more for a rest than to learn about the wine. The place is fabulous and our corner room was stunning with floor to ceiling windows offering spectacular views over the surrounding lush green hills and vineyards. The food was good although not exceptional and too repetitive if you're staying longer than 2 days. The hotel has been overly designed and is not really practical - the showers in the rooms are 'open' showers with no surround so the water goes everywhere ( however housekeeping are very good about cleaning the room whenever you want). Also the terrace in the dining room can accommodate 4 tables only. At lunch time this is a problem as even if the hotel is quiet with 7 rooms occupied, you find yourself scrambling for a table between 1-2pm - this is not the sort of place that serves a quick lunch by the pool - and you are forced to eat inside which is not ideal on a lovely hot day. Also there is no-one offering service by the pool - only occasionally does someone come down to see if you want a drink - so if you need to move a heavy chair or umbrella, you do it yourself! None of this would matter if we were not paying exceedingly high rates to stay here but at the prices charged, service should be top notch. Activities were well organized and there was ample opportunity to explore the 10,000 acre property which was great. We went hiking, mountain biking, horse riding and had a tour of the winery all of which were fabulous. Well worth visiting!

review_text: What an experience! Having spent a couple of days deciding between different tour operators we definitely made the right choice in Cruz andina. review_text: What an experience! My girlfriend and I went on the Old Santiago tour and the Wine-bike tour in late May 2009. A must go, if you enjoy biking and a tour guide (Andres) that is so passionate about Santiago and the surrounds. It's no wonder this is the #1 attraction in Santiago, Chile. Old Santiago Tour: Andres is all about demonstrating both sides of the city. A mixture of the beautiful and picturesque is contrasted with the scars left behind from Santiago's sometimes brutal recent history. Being an architect, Andres pays special attention to how the various structures and buildings around town were made. The trip is well paced, very safe, and is very suited to cyclists of all levels. This tour is best enjoyed early on in your trip to Santiago so that you may have time to go back through the city and revisit the places you enjoyed the most. Wine tour: Andres again has devised a tour that demonstrates contrasts. First off, the tour starts at the El Magnolio Bed and Breakfast in Pirque, about a 45 min drive outside the city. We were treated to a wonderful breakfast which served as a good fuel for the bike ride to come. The house is simply magnificent and the owner is lovely and welcoming. You arrive at Concha y Toro (a very large winery with plenty of tours and tourist visitors) for a tour and wine tasting (you get to keep your tasting glass too, as a parting gift, and it's of really good quality). The bike ride thereafter is a bit long for some bikers, but very flat, on a paved road, and with very little traffic, if at all. There are stops along the way to mention some of the nearby houses and other wineries. This was the ride where you could really relax and enjoy the mountain scenery that surrounded you. You arrive at Vina William Fevre (a small winery, closed to tourism) for an exclusive look at the production facility, a bike ride around the actual grape vines (even taste some grapes if they're growing). The lunch at the winemaker's property was fantastic and you could enjoy some bottles of Vina Fevre wine. Both the Old Santiago and Wine tours were in small groups (4 people). Upon returning to Chile I would not hesitate to book another tour with Andres again.

review_text: Most people do this as a late afternoon tour, ending at sunset. I'm sure that's very pretty, but the crowds must be terrible. We went on mountain bikes, starting early and leaving at around 4pm just as dozens and dozens of minibus tours arrived in one massive convoy. Before that, there were only around 15 other people we saw all day. Give it a full day, start early when it's nice and cool, walk up the big dune, go in the canyon and the tunnel carved by the wind. Take as much water as you can carry - there is nothing available in the valley itself, although there are a couple of shelters which are essential for a little respite from the sun. The whole road up the valley is passable by mountain bike, apart from one tiny stretch which was covered in soft sand. Leave by 4pm, and you'll have the place almost to yourself.

I wouldn't recommend it for anyone who isn't in good health or has mobility issues. But if you're moderately healthy, it's a great experience to immerse yourself in the beautiful Chilean countryside. review_text: Of all the places I visited during my week in Santiago, this museum has stayed with me the most. It’s extremely well done, starting on the ground floor with the global context of peace & reconciliation committees around the world, before moving up to the next 2 floors that deal specifically with the Pinochet regime, from the initial coup, to the referendum that saw democracy restored. The information is brought to life in vivid detail with media footage, newspaper front pages, personal testimonies and many personal items from those who suffered under the regime. I chose to go there because I’m interested in political history but of course, once you’re there, it’s impossible not to be moved and upset by the information & testimony of victims of torture, and the children of disappeared parents. All of this was handled as sensitively as it could be, with a memorial space to sit and reflect. Another aspect that I think made it so interesting and widely relevant is that the museum does a good job of giving the global context as well. We learnt about the roles played throughout the regimes duration by other countries, and I was interested in the wall that told how specific countries around the world reacted to the numbers of Chileans seeking political refuge. My only complaint, and it’s a tiny one, was that I was so bowled over by the museum I really wanted to talk through some of the things I’d read and ask a couple of questions but the only staff I could find were at the front desk, who were completely disinterested in talking. My comment that it was a fascinating museum to the man collecting the audio guides just met with a curt yes, before turning his back on me (we spoke in spanish so it wasn’t a language issue.) My top tip would be to take the audio tour unless you’re completely fluent in Spanish as you don’t want to miss out on any of the details, and some panels are only written in Spanish. It’s also worth knowing there’s a fairly nice cafe within the complex, and it’s easily accessible by metro.

review_text: We took the 3pm tour with Franklin on a Saturday. The weekend seemed to be a good choice since the otherwise frantic city center is much more calm. Well, except for the specific Saturday we ended up picking since we ran into a huge Bolivian carneval parade ;) Anyway, the stops of the tour represented a good mixture of "serious" (i.e. places of historic significance - and frequently tragedy) and "entertaining" (trendy neighborhoods, viewpoints etc.). During the highly informative and pleasant 3 1/2h tour Franklin managed to do the near impossible: One one hand he left no doubt about his own qualms with the Pinochet era, the fact that Chile still has the same constitution from back then, and the negative consequences of that fact for current society. On the other hand he always gave room to opposing views without ever suggesting that they don't possess credibility. Combined with the various other insights he provided, this gave us a feeling of true authenticity. While it was obvious that certain deals exist with a few vendors and restaurant owners along the way, there was never any hard selling during the tour. Only a super-quick pitch and on we went. The tour included a scheduled 30min stop at a restaurant, but when no one opted for it, Franklin continued right away and seemed happy to do so, supporting the overall impression that (even the non-paying) customer is king. Nice! In sum: Highly recommendable! Go for it on your first day in the city.

review_text: My wife and I were staying in a wooden chalet near the base of the mountain, so were able to make the short drive to the volcano easily in our hire-car. There was a steep but well-maintained tarmac road to the ski-station, from where the chair lift took us to an intermediate level of the mountain. From here we went for an hour long walk around an interesting side vent volcano. We then, after a picnic lunch on the slopes, took another chair-lift almost to the snow-line. From the upper station it was a 20 minute walk up to view an area of outstanding beauty, with an active glacier grinding away quite close-by us. We did not venture on to the ice itself, as we only had simple boots. Instead we went for a slightly lower level walk around the wonderful volcanic scenery to another sub-peak. We spent 6 hours in total up the mountain, the highlight of our months tour of Chile.

review_text: There are plenty of boats leaving regularly, at least during the summer time holidays. So we left within a few minutes of getting on board. The cruise goes around the harbour, which is not that special, but for the many sunbathing sea lions on the top of several buoys. We were at the right time of the year to also see the medusa, a very large squid (non dangerous they assured us). Near the harbour there are also many pelicans, and from the boat you have a good view over the town. One stop, mostly for Chileans, is the buoy indicating the location were the Esmeralda sunk, taking with it Arturo Prat, one of the great military heroes of Chile. One can visit a replica of the Esmeralda (a museum) near the harbour or caleta.

review_text: I had a fabulous day tour with Leo. We left my hotel at 8am and spent the day wandering around the port city and cruising around the hills looking at murals and gloriously painted houses. Leo is a photographer and he had lots of great suggestions about how to take superb shots. After about 6 hours wandering and taking photos, Leo took me to one of the very nice local wineries for lunch. I had a splurge and had the tasting menu with matching wines. It was lovely sitting outside in a very relaxed unhassled environment. Leo was superb company and we talked all day about the history of Valparaiso and also his life adventures. On the way home we got talking about Pisco sours (delicious local cocktails). I asked if we could go to a supermarket and get some supplies for my colleagues who would be joining me the next day. Leo had a better idea - he said that because the next day was his day off, he would come and make Pisco sours for my friends. So last night he came to the hotel with pisco, limes, sugar and glasses - all the party essentials.It was such a lovely thing for him to do. Everyone had a really great time. I think says a lot about what a genuinely nice and interesting person Leo is and I would thoroughly recommend his tours. Not only is he well organised, well informed and a great host and I would thoroughly recommend his tours.

review_text: We turned up here on spec having read that we could do a tour. We had just missed the start of one and were walked round to where it was - no hanging around. The guide was very friendly and keen to make sure we all understood. She spoke a little english but the tour was officially in spanish. The group was two scottish, one american and two french (who spoke some spanish). She did a great job of keeping us all engaged. They also had a fig tree part way round the tour and didn't mind at all when I grabbed a few - delicious. The tour was a little more in depth than the one we had done at Mistral the day before and significant effort went into helping us understand what she was trying to say. At the end we tasted two pisco based sweet drinks (mango+pisco and blueberry+pisco) plus two piscos (a clear one and an oak aged one). The pisco was nice (but I would say personally that I thought the Mistral was a little nicer) and you can't complain for free. As with other places there was no pressure to buy anything after the tour (but everyone did buy a bottle of something). It's a little out of the way to get here. We got the bus to drop us on the main road and then walked a kilometer or so up to the pisqueria. I'm sure taxis were available for little cost if you prefer.

review_text: Signed up for a jaunt up to the summit of Volcan Osorno with Huella Andina. It was unexpectedly more of an adventure than I anticipated and it was also awesome. Apparently only about 500 people do this summit a year, including guides, and when we got up there I had the spectacular views all to myself. We also saw sunrise on the way up which was a beauty. Yes, it's not cheap at all! But against all preceding expectations I ended up thing it was money well spent. There is a government mandated limit of 2 people per guide, and it takes about 10 hours to do, plus my guide was rated 10/10 by me, so I could see where the money was going. It is not a technical assent - unless you request it to be! - but you will need crampons and an ice axe (supplied). Also, I know other people have written that it was really hard, but I didn't believe them, and I was out at the pub until perhaps 3 hours before collection for the trip. Mmm... mistake. It is quite hard even if you think you are fit. You need some sensible polar gear. You should also build some redundancy into your trip to make sure you can go up on a good weather day. Enjoy!

review_text: This was a great 1 day tour of Patagonia from the Chile side. Our guide Juan Pablo (aka JP) was awesome and explained everything in spanish and english. The driver Alex also was really good.
